what_it_does: Dynamic RAM (DRAM) — the main memory chips inside computers and servers — is vulnerable to an attack called RowHammer: repeatedly reading from one row of memory cells can inadvertently flip bits in neighboring rows, potentially corrupting data or allowing an attacker to gain unauthorized access. Memory makers and system designers defend against this by measuring how many repeated reads it takes before a row fails (the 'read disturbance threshold') and applying mitigations when that threshold is approached. This paper reveals that a given row's threshold is not a fixed number — it fluctuates significantly over time, and the true worst-case threshold for a row may only appear after nearly 100,000 repeated measurements on the same row. On some chips the worst-case threshold is 3.5 times lower than the best-case observed in early measurements, meaning mitigations calibrated on a small number of measurements are dangerously optimistic. The study covers 160 DDR4 chips and 4 high-bandwidth memory chips (a type of chip that stacks memory layers for speed) from three manufacturers.
